```{r setup}
`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) y else x

# Helper function to escape LaTeX special characters in captions
latex_escape <- function(text) {
  text <- gsub("\\\\", "\\\\textbackslash{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("([#$%&_{}])", "\\\\\\1", text)
  text <- gsub("~", "\\\\textasciitilde{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("\\^", "\\\\textasciicircum{}", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("$\approx$", "$\\\\approx$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("×", "$\\\\times$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("Δ", "$\\\\Delta$", text, fixed = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("–", "--", text, fixed = TRUE)  # en dash
  text <- gsub("—", "---", text, fixed = TRUE)  # em dash
  text <- gsub("'", "`", text, fixed = TRUE)  # left single quote
  text <- gsub("'", "'", text, fixed = TRUE)  # right single quote
  text <- gsub('"', "``", text, fixed = TRUE)  # left double quote
  text <- gsub('"', "''", text, fixed = TRUE)  # right double quote
  return(text)
}

# Helper: figure path resolution
# Returns PNG for HTML output, PDF for DOCX output
fig_path <- function(fig_name) {
  # Get base name without extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(fig_name)
  
  # Detect output format - try multiple methods
  output_format <- NULL
  
  # Method 1: Check if we're rendering to LaTeX/PDF (most important for path resolution)
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    output_format <- "latex"
  }
  
  # Method 2: Check knitr's pandoc output format (most reliable)
  if (is.null(output_format)) {
    pandoc_to <- knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to")
    if (!is.null(pandoc_to)) {
      output_format <- pandoc_to
    }
  }
  
  # Method 3: Check if we're in a DOCX rendering context
  # Quarto sets this in the knitr options
  if (is.null(output_format)) {
    # Check for DOCX-specific indicators
    docx_indicators <- c(
      knitr::opts_knit$get("quarto.document.format") == "docx",
      grepl("docx", knitr::opts_knit$get("out.format") %||% "", ignore.case = TRUE)
    )
    if (any(docx_indicators, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      output_format <- "docx"
    }
  }
  
  png_name <- paste0(base_name, ".png")
  pdf_name <- paste0(base_name, ".pdf")
  jpg_name <- paste0(base_name, ".jpg")
  
  # Find the actual file location
  png_abs <- NULL
  pdf_abs <- NULL
  jpg_abs <- NULL
  
  candidates_png <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", png_name)
  )
  
  candidates_pdf <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name)
  )
  
  candidates_jpg <- c(
    file.path(proj_root, "output/figures", jpg_name),
    file.path("output/figures", jpg_name),
    file.path("../output/figures", jpg_name)
  )
  
  for (path in candidates_png) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      png_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  for (path in candidates_pdf) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      pdf_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  for (path in candidates_jpg) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      jpg_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  # Choose format based on output type
  # For LaTeX: paths need to work for both R execution (with root.dir) and LaTeX compilation
  # Solution: return paths relative to root.dir for R validation, but use a wrapper in include_graphics
  # that handles LaTeX path conversion
  is_latex <- knitr::is_latex_output()
  
  if (exists("use_relative_paths") && use_relative_paths) {
    if (is_latex) {
      # LaTeX: return paths relative to reports/ directory (where LaTeX runs)
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name))
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", png_name))
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(file.path("../output/figures", jpg_name))
      }
    } else {
      # HTML/DOCX: Return relative paths from root.dir (which is set to project root)
      if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
        if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", pdf_name))
        } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", png_name))
        } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", jpg_name))
        }
      } else {
        # HTML: prefer PNG
        if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", png_name))
        } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", jpg_name))
        } else if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
          return(file.path("output/figures", pdf_name))
        }
      }
    }
  } else {
    # Return absolute paths when root.dir is not set
    if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(pdf_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(png_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(jpg_abs)
      }
    } else {
      if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
        return(pdf_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
        return(png_abs)
      } else if (!is.null(jpg_abs)) {
        return(jpg_abs)
      }
    }
  }
  
  # Fallback: return relative path even if file doesn't exist (let LaTeX/Quarto handle error)
  warning("Figure not found: ", fig_name, " (checked: ", paste(c(candidates_pdf, candidates_png), collapse = ", "), ")")
  if (is_latex) {
    return(file.path("../output/figures", pdf_name))
  } else {
    return(file.path("output/figures", if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) pdf_name else png_name))
  }
}

# Wrapper for include_graphics that handles LaTeX path issues
include_graphics_safe <- function(fig_path_result) {
  # For LaTeX with root.dir set, fig_path() returns "../output/figures/..." 
  # which works for LaTeX but knitr::include_graphics() validates relative to root.dir
  # Use error=FALSE to skip validation since we know the file exists (we checked in fig_path)
  knitr::include_graphics(fig_path_result, error = FALSE)
}

# Helper: safe read
sread <- function(path) {
  # Ensure path is a single character string
  if (length(path) > 1) {
    path <- path[1]  # Take first if multiple
  }
  if (length(path) == 1 && is.character(path) && file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch(read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)
  } else {
    NULL
  }
}

  if (file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch({
      pupil_data <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
      # Standardize column names
      if ("sub" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(subject_id = as.character(sub))
      }
      if ("effort" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>%
          mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
            effort == "High" ~ "High_40_MVC",
            effort == "Low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
            TRUE ~ as.character(effort)
          ))
      }
      # Map difficulty level from stimulus_intensity and isOddball
      if ("stimulus_intensity" %in% names(pupil_data) && "isOddball" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            isOddball == 0 | is.na(isOddball) | stimulus_intensity == 0 ~ "Standard",
            # Based on mapping: 0=Standard, 4=Easy, 3=Easy, 1-2=Hard
            stimulus_intensity == 4 ~ "Easy",
            stimulus_intensity == 3 ~ "Easy",
            stimulus_intensity %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Hard",
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          ))
      }
      # Map cognitive_auc column name (cog_auc_w3 for Chapter 3 primary, or cog_auc, or cognitive_auc)
      if ("cog_auc_w3" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"cognitive_auc" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        # Chapter 3 uses W3.0 window (cog_auc_w3) as primary TEPR metric
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(cognitive_auc = cog_auc_w3)
      } else if ("cog_auc" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"cognitive_auc" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(cognitive_auc = cog_auc)
      }
      # Map baseline_B0 column name
      if ("baseline_B0_mean" %in% names(pupil_data) && !"baseline_B0" %in% names(pupil_data)) {
        pupil_data <- pupil_data %>% mutate(baseline_B0 = baseline_B0_mean)
      }
      # Data loaded successfully (diagnostic messages suppressed for rendering)
      break
    }, error = function(e) {
      # Error loading from this path, try next (messages suppressed for rendering)
      NULL
    })
  }

behavioral_data_paths <- c(
  file.path(proj_root, "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL_full.csv"),
  file.path(proj_root, "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL.csv"),

  file.path(proj_root, "data/raw/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),

  "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL_full.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/BAP_analysis_ready_BEHAVIORAL.csv",
  "data/analysis_ready/behavioral_data.csv"
)

behavioral_data <- NULL
for (path in behavioral_data_paths) {
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    tryCatch({
      behavioral_data <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
      # Standardize column names
      if ("subject_id" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(sub = as.character(subject_id))
      }
      if ("task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(task = case_when(
            task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
            task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
          ))
      }
      if ("same_diff_resp_secs" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(rt = same_diff_resp_secs)
      } else if ("resp1RT" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(rt = resp1RT)
      }
      if ("resp_is_correct" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>% mutate(iscorr = as.integer(resp_is_correct))
      }
      # Map effort_condition from grip_level
      if ("grip_level" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
            grip_level == "low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
            grip_level == "high" ~ "High_40_MVC",
            TRUE ~ as.character(grip_level)
          ))
      }
      # Map difficulty_level from stim_offset and stim_is_diff
      # Standard: stim_is_diff = FALSE or stim_offset = 0
      # Hard: Small offsets that are hard to distinguish from Standard
      #   ADT: 8 Hz and 16 Hz
      #   VDT: 0.06 and 0.12 contrast
      # Easy: Large offsets that are easy to distinguish from Standard
      #   ADT: 32 Hz and 64 Hz
      #   VDT: 0.24 and 0.48 contrast
      if ("stim_offset" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        # Ensure task column exists for mapping
        if (!"task" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
            mutate(task = case_when(
              task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
              task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
              TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
            ))
        }
        
        # Create task_type helper column for mapping
        if ("task" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- case_when(
            behavioral_data$task == "ADT" ~ "ADT",
            behavioral_data$task == "VDT" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ NA_character_
          )
        } else if ("task_modality" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- case_when(
            behavioral_data$task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
            behavioral_data$task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
            TRUE ~ NA_character_
          )
        } else {
          behavioral_data$task_type <- NA_character_
        }
        
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            # Standard trials
            stim_is_diff == FALSE | is.na(stim_offset) | stim_offset == 0 ~ "Standard",
            # ADT Easy: 32 or 64 Hz
            task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(32, 64) ~ "Easy",
            # ADT Hard: 8 or 16 Hz
            task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(8, 16) ~ "Hard",
            # VDT Easy: 0.24 or 0.48 contrast
            task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.24, 0.48) ~ "Easy",
            # VDT Hard: 0.06 or 0.12 contrast
            task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.06, 0.12) ~ "Hard",
            # Fallback: infer from magnitude if stim_is_diff is TRUE
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset >= 30 ~ "Easy",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset < 30 & stim_offset > 0 ~ "Hard",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset >= 0.2 ~ "Easy",
            stim_is_diff == TRUE & !is.na(stim_offset) & stim_offset > 0 & 
              task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset < 0.2 & stim_offset > 0 ~ "Hard",
            # Default to Standard
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          )) %>%
          select(-task_type)  # Remove temporary column
      } else if ("stim_level_index" %in% names(behavioral_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(behavioral_data)) {
        # Fallback: use stim_level_index if stim_offset not available
        # NOTE: Please confirm this mapping - typically: 0=Standard, 4=Easy, 2=Hard
        behavioral_data <- behavioral_data %>%
          mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
            stim_is_diff == FALSE | stim_level_index == 0 ~ "Standard",
            stim_level_index == 4 ~ "Easy",
            stim_level_index %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Hard",
            stim_level_index == 3 ~ "Easy",
            TRUE ~ "Standard"
          ))
      }
      
      # Check if difficulty_level already exists but Easy trials are missing
      # If so, try to load from raw data file to get Easy trials
      if ("difficulty_level" %in% names(behavioral_data) && 
          !any(behavioral_data$difficulty_level == "Easy", na.rm = TRUE)) {
        # Try to load raw data file to get Easy trials
        raw_data_paths <- c(
          file.path(proj_root, "data/raw/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
          file.path(proj_root, "../bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"),
          "/Users/mohdasti/Documents/LC-BAP/BAP/Nov2025/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"
        )
        for (raw_path in raw_data_paths) {
          if (file.exists(raw_path)) {
            tryCatch({
              raw_data <- read_csv(raw_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
              # Check if raw data has Easy trials
              if ("stim_offset" %in% names(raw_data) && "stim_is_diff" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                # Map difficulty for raw data
                if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                    mutate(task = case_when(
                      task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                      task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                      TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
                    ))
                }
                if ("task" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data$task_type <- case_when(
                    raw_data$task == "ADT" ~ "ADT",
                    raw_data$task == "VDT" ~ "VDT",
                    TRUE ~ NA_character_
                  )
                } else if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                  raw_data$task_type <- case_when(
                    raw_data$task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                    raw_data$task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                    TRUE ~ NA_character_
                  )
                } else {
                  raw_data$task_type <- NA_character_
                }
                raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                  mutate(difficulty_level = case_when(
                    stim_is_diff == FALSE | is.na(stim_offset) | stim_offset == 0 ~ "Standard",
                    task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(32, 64) ~ "Easy",
                    task_type == "ADT" & stim_offset %in% c(8, 16) ~ "Hard",
                    task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.24, 0.48) ~ "Easy",
                    task_type == "VDT" & stim_offset %in% c(0.06, 0.12) ~ "Hard",
                    TRUE ~ "Standard"
                  )) %>%
                  select(-task_type)
                
                # If raw data has Easy trials, combine with processed data
                if (any(raw_data$difficulty_level == "Easy", na.rm = TRUE)) {
                  # Standardize column names to match behavioral_data
                  if ("subject_id" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>% mutate(sub = as.character(subject_id))
                  }
                  if ("task_modality" %in% names(raw_data) && !"task" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                      mutate(task = case_when(
                        task_modality == "aud" ~ "ADT",
                        task_modality == "vis" ~ "VDT",
                        TRUE ~ as.character(task_modality)
                      ))
                  }
                  if ("resp_is_correct" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>% mutate(accuracy = as.numeric(resp_is_correct))
                  }
                  if ("grip_level" %in% names(raw_data)) {
                    raw_data <- raw_data %>%
                      mutate(effort_condition = case_when(
                        grip_level == "low" ~ "Low_5_MVC",
                        grip_level == "high" ~ "High_40_MVC",
                        TRUE ~ as.character(grip_level)
                      ))
                  }
                  
                  # Combine: keep all rows from processed data, add Easy trials from raw data
                  behavioral_data <- bind_rows(
                    behavioral_data,
                    raw_data %>% filter(difficulty_level == "Easy")
                  )
                  break
                }
              }
            }, error = function(e) {
              # Silently continue if raw data can't be loaded
            })
          }
        }
      }
      
      break
    }, error = function(e) {
      cat("Error loading", path, ":", e$message, "\n")
      NULL
    })
  }
}

# Derive simple pass/fail summaries
pf_subj <- if (!is.null(ppc_subj_cens)) {
  if ("any_flag" %in% names(ppc_subj_cens)) {
    ppc_subj_cens %>% 
      summarise(n_cells = n(), n_flagged = sum(any_flag, na.rm=TRUE), 
                pct_flagged = round(100*mean(any_flag, na.rm=TRUE),1))
  } else {
    ppc_subj_cens %>% 
      mutate(any_flag = (qp_rmse_midbody > 0.09) | (ks_mean > 0.15)) %>%
      summarise(n_cells = n(), n_flagged = sum(any_flag, na.rm=TRUE), 
                pct_flagged = round(100*mean(any_flag, na.rm=TRUE),1))
  }
} else tibble(n_cells=NA, n_flagged=NA, pct_flagged=NA)

pf_uncond <- if (!is.null(ppc_uncond_cens)) {
  if ("any_flag" %in% names(ppc_uncond_cens)) {
    ppc_uncond_cens %>% 
      summarise(n_cells = n(), n_flagged = sum(any_flag, na.rm=TRUE), 
                pct_flagged = round(100*mean(any_flag, na.rm=TRUE),1))
  } else {
    ppc_uncond_cens %>% 
      mutate(any_flag = (qp_rmse_midbody > 0.09) | (ks_mean > 0.15)) %>%
      summarise(n_cells = n(), n_flagged = sum(any_flag, na.rm=TRUE), 
                pct_flagged = round(100*mean(any_flag, na.rm=TRUE),1))
  }
} else tibble(n_cells=NA, n_flagged=NA, pct_flagged=NA)
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

This chapter presents a hierarchical Wiener diffusion decision model (DDM) for a response-signal change-detection task in older adults. The primary model maps task difficulty to drift rate ($v$) and boundary separation ($a$), with starting-point bias ($z$) varying by task and effort but constant across difficulty levels (reflecting the randomized trial design), and small condition effects on non-decision time ($t_0$). Results showed that high-effort (40% MVC) conditions reduced drift rate ($v$) and increased non-decision time ($t_0$) relative to low-effort (5% MVC) conditions, consistent with resource competition and cognitive-motor interference. Contrary to predictions from adaptive caution theories, boundary separation ($a$) did not increase under high effort. Trial-wise pupil-linked arousal (TEPR) did not reliably modulate drift rate or starting-point bias when included as predictors. We report comprehensive quality assurance checks, manipulation checks independent of the DDM, model comparison via LOO cross-validation, and extensive posterior predictive checks with emphasis on subject-wise mid-body RT quantiles.

\newpage

# Introduction

## Age-Related Slowing and Strategic Adaptation in Decision-Making

A hallmark of cognitive aging is a pervasive slowing of response times across virtually all task domains. Older adults consistently take longer to respond in speeded decision tasks than younger adults, a phenomenon historically interpreted as *generalized slowing* [@birren1965age; @salthouse1985speed]. Classic analyses using Brinley plots [@brinley1965cognitive] supported the idea of a global factor that uniformly slows processing with age [@cerella1985; @salthouse1996]. In fact, increased age is associated with a decrease in the speed of many mental operations, as posited by the processing-speed theory of cognitive aging [@salthouse1996]. According to this view, slower processing leaves less time for higher-order operations, effectively creating a bottleneck in available cognitive resources. However, simply viewing aging as a uniform "slower clock speed" obscures important nuances. Older adults often maintain accuracy rates comparable to younger adults by adjusting their decision-making strategy: they tend to respond more cautiously, emphasizing accuracy over speed. In other words, rather than being a passive consequence of a slower brain, longer response times in older people can reflect an active, strategic adaptation aimed at preserving accuracy in the face of cognitive and neural challenges. Empirical evidence for this adaptive strategy comes from speed--accuracy tradeoff studies showing that, when given the option, older adults favor slower, more accurate responding, whereas younger adults are willing to respond faster at the cost of more errors [@ratcliff2004aging; @starns2010; @rabbitt1979old]. This age-related shift toward a "slow but sure" decision mode is often interpreted as an adaptive mechanism: older adults may consciously or unconsciously slow down to avoid mistakes, compensating for declines in sensory or cognitive processing by "buying" extra decision time [@mata2007aging; @ratcliff2006aging].

Notably, this cautious response style means that aging effects on decision performance are not uniform across all components of processing. Contemporary cognitive aging models distinguish between generalized slowing and component-specific changes in decision dynamics. For example, older adults experience sensory and perceptual degradations, often conceptualized as a reduction in neural signal-to-noise ratio [@li2001aging; @lindenberger1994sensory], as well as distinct motor slowing [@seidler2010motor], which each can prolong portions of the response time independent of decision strategy. Simultaneously, older adults exhibit changes in decision criteria, such as setting a higher threshold for required evidence before responding [@ratcliff2001aging; @ratcliff2004aging; @ratcliff2007application; @ratcliff2008diffusion]. This raises an important question: does aging slow core cognitive processing speed, or do older adults simply recalibrate their speed--accuracy tradeoff by becoming more cautious? The answer appears to be a combination of both, depending on task demands. In relatively simple perceptual decision tasks—such as brightness discrimination or letter identification—healthy older adults often achieve accuracy similar to young adults by adopting conservative decision thresholds and taking more time, rather than by processing information more efficiently [@ratcliff2001aging; @ratcliff2003diffusion]. Critically, drift rates (the quality of evidence accumulation) are preserved in these simple perceptual tasks, indicating that fundamental cognitive processing capacity remains intact when task demands are low. In contrast, under more challenging conditions—specifically episodic memory tasks requiring recollection of contextual details [@spaniol2006] or complex visual searches requiring serial attention allocation [@madden1991]—older adults exhibit genuine declines in drift rates. This indicates real reductions in the quality of decision-driving information. Thus, while slower responses in simple tasks reflect a strategic emphasis on accuracy (criterion shift) and slower peripheral processes, complex tasks reveal a different pattern. When cognitive demands exceed the older brain's capacity, seniors often cannot maintain the same quality of evidence accumulation as the young, leading to performance decrements when they attempt to respond quickly. These findings underscore that aging impacts decision-making through multiple pathways: a general tendency toward slower, more cautious responding, coupled with task-specific deficits in processing efficiency when cognitive demands are high.

## Insights from Drift-Diffusion Modeling of Aging

To disentangle these component processes of decision-making, researchers increasingly turn to computational modeling approaches. One powerful framework is the Drift Diffusion Model (DDM), which provides a quantitative decomposition of choice reaction time data into psychologically interpretable parameters [@ratcliff1978theory; @ratcliff2008diffusion; @voss2004interpreting]. In a forced-choice decision task, the DDM conceptualizes the process as a gradual, noisy accumulation of evidence toward one of two decision boundaries (representing the response options). The key model parameters include:

-   **Drift rate ($v$)** – the average speed of evidence accumulation toward the correct decision. This reflects the quality or efficiency of information processing; a higher drift rate means the decision maker can extract and use task-relevant information more quickly.
-   **Decision boundary ($a$)** – the amount of evidence required to commit to a choice, often interpreted as response caution or threshold. A larger boundary separation indicates a more cautious strategy (waiting for more evidence before deciding), whereas a smaller boundary implies a more impulsive or speed-emphasizing strategy.
-   **Starting point ($z$)** – the initial bias or predisposition toward one option or the other before evidence is accumulated. If the starting point is centered (typically 0.5 in relative units), there is no pre-existing bias; deviations from center indicate an a priori bias to favor a particular response (e.g., a bias to say "yes" vs "no" in a detection task).
-   **Non-decision time ($t_0$)** – the duration of processes outside of the evidence accumulation itself, such as perceptual encoding of the stimulus and the motor execution of the response [@voss2004interpreting]. Non-decision time accounts for aspects of the reaction time that are not decision-related.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ddm-process
#| fig-cap: "Drift Diffusion Model: Evidence Accumulation Process. The DDM models decision-making as a noisy evidence accumulation process. Evidence accumulates from a starting point ($z$, starting-point bias) toward one of two decision boundaries: the upper boundary corresponds to \"different\" responses, and the lower boundary to \"same\" responses. The rate of evidence accumulation is determined by the drift rate ($v$), which reflects the quality of the stimulus evidence. The distance between boundaries is the boundary separation ($a$), which reflects response caution. The total reaction time (RT) is the sum of non-decision time ($t_0$, reflecting perceptual encoding and motor execution) and the decision time (time to reach a boundary). In this example, the starting point is biased toward the upper boundary ($z > 0.5$), and positive drift leads to a \"different\" response."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "90%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("fig_ddm_process.pdf"))
```

Formally, the evidence accumulation process follows the stochastic differential equation [@ratcliff1978theory; @ratcliff2008diffusion]:

$$dX(t) = v \, dt + dW(t)$$ {#eq-sde}

where $X(t)$ is the accumulated evidence at time $t$, $v$ is the drift rate (evidence strength), and $dW(t)$ is a Wiener noise process with unit variance. The process starts at $X(0) = z \cdot a$, where $z \in [0,1]$ is the starting-point bias (expressed as a proportion of boundary separation) and $a > 0$ is the boundary separation [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The decision process terminates when $X(t)$ reaches either the upper boundary ($X(t) = a$) or the lower boundary ($X(t) = 0$). The total reaction time (RT) is the sum of the decision time and the non-decision time ($t_0$):

$$\text{RT} = t_{\text{decision}} + t_0$$ {#eq-rt}

By fitting the DDM to participants' accuracy and response time distributions, one can infer how these latent parameters differ between groups (e.g. young vs. old) or conditions. This model-based approach has proved especially illuminating in aging research. Rather than relying on overall slowing measures alone, the DDM allows researchers to pinpoint which aspects of processing slow down or change with age and which remain intact.

The DDM mathematically formalizes the behavioral patterns described above. The model confirms that older adults' slower responses are largely due to shifts in caution and peripheral processing, rather than uniformly impaired evidence accumulation. Specifically, older adults consistently exhibit significantly higher decision thresholds ($a$) than younger adults across a variety of tasks [@ratcliff2004aging; @ratcliff2008diffusion], quantitatively capturing the strategic slowing: by widening the distance between boundaries, older adults counteract internal noise and maintain high accuracy. Additionally, the model isolates the contribution of peripheral slowing; older adults typically show increased non-decision times ($t_0$), often 80–100 ms longer than young adults [@ratcliff2004aging], reflecting age-related delays in motor execution and sensory encoding. Crucially, the DDM reveals that drift rate ($v$)—the core measure of cognitive processing efficiency—is often remarkably preserved in aging for simple perceptual tasks [@ratcliff2001aging; @ratcliff2003diffusion; @ratcliff2004aging].

However, as noted previously, this preservation is not universal: in tasks taxing memory retrieval [@spaniol2006] or complex visual search [@madden1991], modeling confirms a decline in drift rates, indicating that for complex cognitive operations, the older brain does accumulate evidence more slowly. Furthermore, while older adults can adjust their boundaries, they often exhibit a rigidity in this setting; Starns and Ratcliff [-@starns2010] demonstrated that older adults fail to lower their boundaries ($a$) optimally under speed pressure, prioritizing accuracy even when the task incentivizes speed. Regarding bias ($z$), healthy aging is generally not associated with systematic shifts in starting point for simple tasks, though specific biases can emerge in memory paradigms (e.g., a conservative bias against "new" items to avoid false alarms) [@spaniol2006; @ratcliff2004aging]. Overall, the application of drift-diffusion modeling provides a nuanced portrait of aging: it mathematically separates the strategic adaptations (increased $a$) and peripheral slowing (increased $t_0$) from the fundamental cognitive capacity (drift rate $v$), which remains intact in simple contexts but declines under high cognitive load. 

Having established the baseline DDM profile of older adults, we turn to an important modulating factor: arousal and effort. In this chapter, we leverage the diffusion model to investigate how fluctuations in arousal (induced via physical effort) can alter these latent decision processes in older adults.

## Arousal, Effort, and Decision Performance in Older Adults

Beyond baseline aging effects, cognitive performance is strongly influenced by the organism's arousal state—the level of alertness or activation of physiological and neural systems. Classic theory, dating back to the Yerkes–Dodson law [@yerkes1908], holds that the relationship between arousal and performance follows an inverted-U function: increasing arousal enhances performance up to an optimal point, after which further arousal (especially if reaching stress or anxiety levels) impairs performance. In the context of aging, this dynamic takes on special significance. Adaptive Gain Theory (AGT) [@astonjones2005] provides a neural mechanism for this relationship, linking phasic and tonic Locus Coeruleus activity to optimal task performance. When this framework is extended to aging, researchers posit that the arousal--performance curve is altered, often manifesting as a leftward shift or compression of the inverted-U function [@mather2016; @mikneviciute2022]. This implies that older adults may reach their "optimal" arousal peak at lower levels of objective demand than younger adults. Consequently, levels of effort or stress that might be engaging or beneficial for a younger adult (placing them at the peak of the curve) can push an older adult onto the "descending limb," leading to supra-optimal arousal and performance decrements [@huang2024; @mather2016].

Older adults typically have a reduced physiological capacity to sustain high arousal yet often need to exert greater mental effort to perform a given task at the same level as a younger person. Recent studies support the idea that effortful engagement is more taxing for older adults in measurable ways. For example, Hess and Ennis [@hess2012] demonstrated that when older adults performed continuous arithmetic tasks (e.g., subtraction), they exhibited significantly larger increases in systolic blood pressure (SBP)—a physiological index of effortful arousal—than young adults, and this elevated physiological cost predicted greater fatigue on subsequent tasks. Furthermore, research directly relevant to the current paradigm has shown that concurrent physical effort can be detrimental to cognition in aging. Azer et al. [@azer2023] found that while maintaining a concurrent moderate isometric handgrip (30% MVC), older adults showed significantly reduced accuracy in a visual working memory task with distractors, whereas younger adults remained unaffected. This supports the limited-capacity framework, suggesting that shared processing resources [@wickens2008] are more easily depleted in older adults, or that the combined demand drives arousal into a dysregulated state [@verhaeghen2003]. However, it remains unclear how these effort- and arousal-related costs translate into the latent mechanisms of decision formation in older adults. Prior work has established that arousal and effort can alter observed performance (accuracy/RT) in aging, but has not directly tested *which computational components* of the decision process are affected (e.g., evidence quality vs. response caution vs. non-decision processes), particularly using a framework that jointly links physiological arousal (pupillometry) to diffusion-model parameters. The present chapter addresses this gap by combining pupillometry with hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling to identify how effort-induced arousal maps onto latent decision parameters in older adults.

What are the expected effects of arousal fluctuations on the decision-making mechanisms of older adults? By applying the drift-diffusion model (DDM), we can make specific hypotheses about how effort-induced arousal will modulate latent decision parameters. The present study manipulates arousal via physical effort (5% vs. 40% MVC), providing a controlled way to "push" older participants along the arousal curve. Behavioral theories such as Resource Competition and Limited Capacity predict that excessive effort will siphon processing resources away from the decision process, degrading evidence quality, whereas Adaptive Gain Theory predicts that older adults will more quickly slide down the descending limb of the inverted-U curve when demands are high. These frameworks collectively motivate the computational predictions outlined after we review the relevant physiological mechanisms. Together, these accounts make distinct, parameter-level predictions about *how* performance should change under effort. If high effort pushes older adults into supra-optimal arousal or resource competition, evidence quality should degrade (lower drift rate, $v$). If pupil-linked arousal functions as a control/conflict signal, older adults may respond more cautiously (higher boundary separation, $a$). If concurrent grip maintenance interferes with encoding or motor output, peripheral processes may slow (higher non-decision time, $t_0$). Finally, if phasic arousal reduces pre-existing response tendencies, starting-point bias may move toward neutrality ($z \rightarrow 0.5$). We test these predictions using hierarchical Bayesian diffusion modeling, and we use pupillometry to index the arousal state that is hypothesized to drive these shifts.



## Arousal Dynamics and the Locus Coeruleus-Norepinephrine System

To ground these parameter-level predictions in physiology, we next focus on the Locus Coeruleus–Norepinephrine (LC–NE) system, a central regulator of arousal and neural gain [@astonjones2005]. Because LC–NE dynamics are observable via pupillometry, this framework provides a mechanistic bridge between effort-induced arousal and diffusion-model parameters. The LC-NE system modulates the "neural gain" of cortical circuits—essentially the signal-to-noise ratio of information processing. According to Adaptive Gain Theory (AGT), optimal performance relies on a balance between two modes of LC activity: a moderate tonic (baseline) firing rate that promotes focused attention, and robust phasic (event-related) bursts that facilitate rapid behavioral responses to task-relevant stimuli [@astonjones2005; @gilzenrat2010].

In aging, LC structure and NE regulation change in ways that can compress the arousal–performance function described above, increasing susceptibility to supra-optimal arousal under demanding conditions [@mather2016; @huang2024]. The LC–NE system provides a mechanistic pathway through which effort-induced arousal can perturb decision computations.

**Pupillometry** provides a powerful, non-invasive window into these LC-NE dynamics. Because pupil diameter tracks LC firing activity with high temporal precision [@joshi2016; @murphy2014], it serves as a proxy for both tonic and phasic arousal states.

-   **Baseline Pupil Diameter:** Reflects tonic LC activity and general alertness levels [@gilzenrat2010].

-   **Task-Evoked Pupil Response (TEPR):** Reflects phasic LC activation and the mobilization of mental effort during task execution [@beatty1982]. Specifically, the amplitude and latency of the TEPR—often quantified as the Area Under the Curve (AUC)—have been linked to the subjective difficulty of a task and the cognitive resources recruited to perform it [@kahneman1966; @vangerven2004].

Crucially, recent computational work has begun to bridge the gap between these physiological arousal signals and the latent cognitive processes of decision-making. In a seminal study, Cavanagh et al. [-@cavanagh2014] demonstrated that eye tracking and pupillometry serve as indicators of dissociable latent decision processes. By applying hierarchical Bayesian DDM to a probabilistic learning task, they found that while gaze dwell time predicted the rate of evidence accumulation (drift rate), **pupil dilation specifically predicted an increase in the decision threshold ($a$)** during high-conflict choices. This finding fundamentally reframed the role of phasic arousal in decision-making: rather than merely "energizing" the system generally, the pupil-linked arousal response can act as a specific signal for cognitive control, prompting a "hold your horses" mechanism [@frank2006] that raises the decision boundary to prevent impulsive errors. This link between pupil dilation and threshold adjustment ($a$) has since been corroborated by others, suggesting it may be a general marker of decision uncertainty and conflict monitoring [@urai2017; @vanderwel2018].

This connection is vital for the present study. By integrating pupillometry with DDM, we can move beyond simple behavioral outcomes to ask mechanistic questions about how physical effort impacts the aging brain. Does the physical arousal from a high-effort handgrip act as a beneficial boost that sharpens neural gain (increasing drift rate, $v$), as Adaptive Gain Theory might predict for moderate arousal? Or, does it trigger a conflict signal that prompts older adults to become more conservative (increasing threshold, $a$), as suggested by the work of Cavanagh et al. [-@cavanagh2014]? Alternatively, if the effort pushes older adults into a supra-optimal state, does the pupil signal reflect internal noise that degrades evidence quality (decreasing $v$)? This combined pupil-DDM approach allows us to directly test these competing accounts by linking observable physiological states to the latent computational components of the decision process. Critically, these frameworks generate separable predictions at the level of diffusion parameters. Resource competition / limited-capacity accounts predict reduced evidence quality under high effort (**$v \downarrow$**). Conflict-control or “hold your horses” accounts predict increased response caution (**$a \uparrow$**) and, potentially, modest slowing outside the decision process due to concurrent motor demands (**$t_0 \uparrow$**). Finally, if phasic LC–NE responses reduce pre-existing response tendencies, starting-point bias may shift toward neutrality (**$z \rightarrow 0.5$**). This parameter-level separability is exactly what motivates the pupil-informed hierarchical Bayesian DDM approach used here and leads directly to the predictions formalized below.


### Hypotheses and Predictions

Grounded in the behavioral and physiological frameworks above, we test four primary predictions.

1. **Drift rate ($v$)** will decrease under high effort (40% MVC) relative to low effort, reflecting degraded evidence accumulation from resource competition or supra-optimal arousal.
2. **Boundary separation ($a$)** will increase under high effort, reflecting the conflict-control signal suggested by phasic pupil-linked arousal and older adults’ strategic caution.
3. **Non-decision time ($t_0$)** may increase modestly under high effort, reflecting cognitive-motor interference during concurrent grip maintenance.
4. **Starting bias ($z$)** may shift toward 0.5 under high effort if strong phasic LC–NE responses reduce pre-existing response tendencies (i.e., a bias “reset”) [@degee2020pupil]. 



## Conclusion and Overview of the Present Study

In this chapter, we investigate how effort-induced arousal modulates decision-making in older adults at a computational level. By applying hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion modeling (HDDM) to behavioral data from older participants under low-effort vs. high-effort conditions, we test whether heightened arousal degrades evidence accumulation, triggers compensatory increases in boundary separation, alters bias, or slows non-decision processes. By decomposing older adults' performance with the DDM, we can pinpoint the locus of the arousal effect: is it degrading the evidence itself, shifting the strategic criterion, resetting biases, or altering peripheral processing speeds? This approach allows us to move beyond simple outcome measures (mean reaction time or accuracy) to visualize the mechanism of how a physiologically loaded aging brain arrives at a choice. The broader significance of this work lies in understanding whether the characteristic cautiousness and processing inefficiencies of older decision-makers are fixed traits or dynamic features modulated by physiological state. If arousal can "tune" decision parameters in predictable ways, it suggests that decision performance in aging is not static but state-dependent. If excessive effort proves detrimental as hypothesized, it highlights the critical importance of effort regulation and stress management for older individuals in demanding environments. Ultimately, by mathematically decomposing these effects, we seek to clarify whether boosting arousal in older adults helps "overclock" their decision processes or instead exacerbates underlying capacity limits. This knowledge contributes to a more comprehensive theory of cognitive aging—one that accounts for both the baseline architectural changes of the brain and the dynamic, moment-to-moment influence of internal physiological states.

@fig-ddm-pipeline provides a conceptual overview of the cross-level mechanistic framework that guides this investigation, illustrating how experimental manipulations (physical effort, task modality, stimulus difficulty) engage the Locus Coeruleus–Norepinephrine (LC–NE) arousal system, which is observable through pupillometry, and how these physiological states map onto latent DDM parameters that ultimately determine behavioral outcomes (accuracy and reaction time).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ddm-pipeline
#| fig-cap: "Cross-Level Mechanism: Effort, Arousal (LC–NE), Pupillometry, and DDM Parameters. Conceptual diagram illustrating the mechanistic framework connecting experimental manipulations (Level 1: physical effort, task modality, stimulus difficulty) to the Locus Coeruleus–Norepinephrine (LC–NE) arousal control system (Level 2), observable through pupillometry signals (Level 3: baseline pupil diameter for tonic arousal, task-evoked pupil response/TEPR for phasic arousal), and their mapping onto latent DDM parameters (Level 4: drift rate v, boundary separation a, starting-point bias z, non-decision time t₀) that determine behavioral outcomes (Level 5: accuracy and reaction time). Color coding differentiates experimental manipulations (blue), LC–NE system (purple), pupillometry signals (green), DDM parameters (orange), and behavioral outcomes (gray). Solid arrows indicate empirically supported relationships; dashed arrows indicate hypothesized or weakly supported relationships. The diagram highlights how physical effort increases physiological demand on the LC–NE system, captured by pupillometry as a non-invasive proxy, and how these arousal states modulate decision-making parameters—particularly the negative effect of high effort on drift rate v through resource competition or supra-optimal arousal, and the minimal effects on boundary separation a and non-decision time t₀."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "90%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("ddm-pipeline"))
```

# Methods

## Participants and Experimental Design

### Participants

Participants were recruited from communities surrounding the University of California, Riverside, through multiple channels including direct mail, posted flyers, social media advertisements, and word-of-mouth referrals. Eligibility criteria required participants to be aged 60–90 years, possess normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, demonstrate sufficient English language comprehension to follow experimental instructions, and exhibit right-hand dominance. Exclusion criteria comprised contraindications for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), current use of psychotropic medications, clinically significant neurological disorders, and major systemic health conditions including diabetes mellitus. 

Sixty-nine individuals initially enrolled in the study. Two participants were excluded following enrollment: one due to suspected mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and another due to possible essential tremor, yielding a final sample of 67 older adults (age: M = 71.3 years, SD = 4.8, range = 65+ years). Sample size was determined through a priori power analysis using G\*Power 3.1 [@faul2007g]. For a repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) comparing two within-subject conditions (low vs. high grip force), assuming a medium effect size (*f* = 0.25), alpha level of 0.05, correlation of 0.5 between repeated measures, and desired statistical power of 0.80, the analysis indicated that a minimum of 34 participants was necessary. Twelve participants performed at or below chance level ($\leq$ 55% accuracy) in some experimental conditions but were retained in analyses to maximize sample size, as hierarchical modeling approaches borrow statistical strength across participants to stabilize individual-level parameter estimates.

All participants provided written informed consent and received either course credit or monetary compensation for their participation. Study procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of California, Riverside, and all experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with approved guidelines and regulations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline Demographics for Each Task After Data Cleaning"
#| tbl-pos: "htbp"
#| echo: false

# Load included participants
included <- read_csv(file.path(p, "qa_subject_inclusion.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
included_ids <- included$subject_id

# Load demographics
demo_path <- "/Users/mohdasti/Documents/LC-BAP/BAP/Nov2025/LC Aging Subject Data master spreadsheet - demographics.csv"
demo <- read_csv(demo_path, skip = 1, show_col_types = FALSE, 
                 col_names = c('study', 'subject_id', 'subject_id2', 'demo_comments', 'completion', 
                              'bap_ses1_date', 'bap_ses2_date', 'bap_ses3_date', 'bap_ses_order',
                              'bap_tablet_date', 'blank1', 'bam_ses1', 'bam_ses2', 'bam_ses3', 'bam_order',
                              'bam_tablet', 'blank2', 'dob', 'age', 'sex', 'edu', 'hand', 'race', 
                              'ethnicity', 'first_lang', 'blank3', 'vision', 'prescription', 'blank4',
                              'neuropsych_comments', 'adt_comments', 'vdt_comments', 'stx_comments',
                              'future_contact', 'blank5', 'days_ses1_2', 'days_ses2_3'))

# Filter for included participants and clean data
demo_filtered <- demo %>%
  filter(subject_id %in% included_ids) %>%
  mutate(
    age = as.numeric(age),
    sex = trimws(tolower(sex)),
    edu = case_when(
      edu == '<12' ~ '11',
      edu == 'less than 12' ~ '11',
      TRUE ~ as.character(edu)
    ),
    edu = as.numeric(edu),
    race = trimws(race),
    ethnicity = trimws(ethnicity)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(age))

# Load neuropsych data for MoCA scores
neuropsych_path <- "/Users/mohdasti/Documents/LC-BAP/BAP/Nov2025/LC Aging Subject Data master spreadsheet - neuropsych.csv"
neuropsych <- read_csv(neuropsych_path, skip = 1, show_col_types = FALSE)
moca_col <- grep('MoCA|moca', names(neuropsych), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]
if (!is.na(moca_col)) {
  neuropsych <- neuropsych %>%
    mutate(
      subject_id = `SUBJECT NUMBER`,
      moca = as.numeric(!!sym(moca_col))
    ) %>%
    select(subject_id, moca)
} else {
  neuropsych <- data.frame(subject_id = character(), moca = numeric())
}

# Load behavioral data to determine task participation
beh_path <- "/Users/mohdasti/Documents/LC-BAP/BAP/Nov2025/bap_beh_trialdata_v3.csv"
beh <- read_csv(beh_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

# Get task participation
task_participation <- beh %>%
  filter(subject_id %in% included_ids) %>%
  mutate(task = case_when(
    task_modality == 'aud' ~ 'ADT',
    task_modality == 'vis' ~ 'VDT',
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(task)) %>%
  distinct(subject_id, task) %>%
  group_by(subject_id) %>%
  summarise(
    has_adt = any(task == 'ADT'),
    has_vdt = any(task == 'VDT'),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Merge with demographics and MoCA
demo_with_tasks <- demo_filtered %>%
  left_join(task_participation, by = 'subject_id') %>%
  left_join(neuropsych, by = 'subject_id')

# Create task-specific datasets
adt_demo <- demo_with_tasks %>% filter(has_adt == TRUE & !is.na(age))
vdt_demo <- demo_with_tasks %>% filter(has_vdt == TRUE & !is.na(age))

# Function to calculate demographics for a dataset
calc_demographics <- function(data) {
  n <- nrow(data)
  
  # Age
  age_mean <- mean(data$age, na.rm = TRUE)
  age_sd <- sd(data$age, na.rm = TRUE)
  age_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', age_mean, age_sd)
  
  # Gender
  female_count <- sum(data$sex == 'female', na.rm = TRUE)
  female_pct <- round(100 * female_count / n, 1)
  gender_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', female_count, female_pct)
  
  # Education
  edu_mean <- mean(data$edu, na.rm = TRUE)
  edu_sd <- sd(data$edu, na.rm = TRUE)
  edu_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', edu_mean, edu_sd)
  
  # MoCA
  if ('moca' %in% names(data)) {
    moca_mean <- mean(data$moca, na.rm = TRUE)
    moca_sd <- sd(data$moca, na.rm = TRUE)
    moca_str <- sprintf('%.1f (%.1f)', moca_mean, moca_sd)
  } else {
    moca_str <- 'N/A'
  }
  
  # Race categorization
  race_clean <- data$race
  has_white <- grepl('white', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE)
  has_black <- grepl('black|african', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE)
  has_asian <- grepl('^asian$|^asian,', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE) & !has_white
  has_other <- grepl('other', race_clean, ignore.case = TRUE) & !has_white & !has_black & !has_asian
  
  race_cat <- rep(NA_character_, length(race_clean))
  race_cat[has_white] <- 'White/Caucasian'
  race_cat[has_black & !has_white] <- 'Black/African American'
  race_cat[has_asian & !has_white & !has_black] <- 'Asian'
  race_cat[has_other & !has_white & !has_black & !has_asian] <- 'Other'
  race_cat[is.na(race_clean)] <- NA_character_
  
  white_count <- sum(race_cat == 'White/Caucasian', na.rm = TRUE)
  white_pct <- round(100 * white_count / n, 1)
  white_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', white_count, white_pct)
  
  black_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Black/African American', na.rm = TRUE)
  black_pct <- round(100 * black_count / n, 1)
  black_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', black_count, black_pct)
  
  asian_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Asian', na.rm = TRUE)
  asian_pct <- round(100 * asian_count / n, 1)
  asian_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', asian_count, asian_pct)
  
  other_count <- sum(race_cat == 'Other', na.rm = TRUE)
  other_pct <- round(100 * other_count / n, 1)
  other_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', other_count, other_pct)
  
  # Hispanic/Latino - fix: exclude "Not Hispanic or Latino"
  hispanic_count <- sum(
    grepl('hispanic|latino', data$ethnicity, ignore.case = TRUE) & 
    !grepl('not hispanic|not latino', data$ethnicity, ignore.case = TRUE),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  hispanic_pct <- round(100 * hispanic_count / n, 1)
  hispanic_str <- sprintf('%d (%.1f%%)', hispanic_count, hispanic_pct)
  
  return(list(
    n = n, age = age_str, gender = gender_str, edu = edu_str, moca = moca_str,
    white = white_str, black = black_str, asian = asian_str, other = other_str,
    hispanic = hispanic_str
  ))
}
```

### Stimuli and Task Design

**Task overview** Participants completed two response-signal same/different discrimination tasks—an Auditory Detection Task (ADT) and a Visual Detection Task (VDT)—each performed under concurrent hand-grip effort manipulation. In both tasks, a standard and probe stimulus were presented in succession, and participants judged whether the stimuli were the same or different using button presses, followed by a confidence rating.

**Trial structure.** Both tasks shared the same response-signal timeline (see @fig-trial-structure). Each trial began with a jittered blank interval (1.5–4.5 s) displaying only a gray background. Participants were then shown a 3-second rectangular grip gauge with a marker positioned at either 5% or 40% from the bottom, indicating the target force level to be maintained using a hand-held dynamometer (left hand) at the corresponding percentage of their maximum voluntary contraction (MVC). MVC was determined during a brief calibration procedure prior to each task. Following the grip period, a 0.25-second blank screen and 0.5-second fixation dot preceded stimulus presentation.

**Auditory Detection Task (ADT).** The standard stimulus was a 0.1-second sinusoidal tone at 1000 Hz. After a 0.5-second inter-stimulus interval, the probe stimulus was presented as a 0.1-second tone that was either identical to the standard ($\Delta frequency$ = 0) or positively offset by $\Delta frequency \in \{8, 16, 32, 64\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. For drift-diffusion model (DDM) analyses, the four non-zero offsets were collapsed into two difficulty bins: Hard = {8, 16} Hz and Easy = {32, 64} Hz, with Standard = 0 Hz.

**Visual Detection Task (VDT).** The standard stimulus was a centrally presented sinusoidal Gabor patch (spatial frequency 1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, diameter 4°, duration 0.1 s). After a 0.5-second inter-stimulus interval, the probe stimulus was presented as a 0.1-second Gabor that was either identical to the standard ($\Delta contrast$ = 0) or showed a positive contrast increase of $\Delta contrast \in \{0.06, 0.12, 0.24, 0.48\}$, with all other parameters held constant. For DDM analyses, offsets were collapsed into Hard = {0.06, 0.12} and Easy = {0.24, 0.48}, with Standard = 0.

**Response collection.** Following stimulus offset, participants relaxed their grip and had a 3-second response window to indicate whether the two stimuli were the same or different using their right hand (index finger = "different"; middle finger = "same"). This was immediately followed by another 3-second window in which participants provided a confidence rating on a 4-point scale (1 = low confidence, 4 = high confidence).

**Trial counts and monitoring.** Each task comprised 150 trials distributed across five blocks of 30 trials each. Within each block, the five stimulus levels (standard plus four offsets) were crossed with the two effort conditions (5% vs. 40% MVC) and presented in pseudorandom order with equal proportions (three repetitions per stimulus × effort combination). Hand-grip performance was monitored after each block, and participants received corrective feedback if they consistently failed to maintain the dynamometer at the designated force level (near the grip gauge marker) and/or for the correct duration (until offset of the probe stimulus).

Each trial includes a jittered pre-cue interval, a 3-s grip-gauge period (low vs high effort), a two-stimulus sequence (standard → delay → probe), followed by a 3-s same/different response window and a 3-s confidence rating. Full stimulus parameters and difficulty binning are described in the Tasks and Conditions section."
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "90%"
include_graphics_safe(fig_path("Trial_Structure.png"))
```

### Equipment

The experimental task was programmed and executed on an Alienware laptop. Visual stimuli were presented via a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies, Montreal, Canada; 480 Hz refresh rate, 1920×1080 resolution) and viewed through a head coil-mounted mirror (viewing distance $\approx$ 12 cm). Auditory stimuli were delivered via MRI-safe earbuds (Newmatic Medical, Duluth, GA; 30 dB NRR). Behavioral responses were recorded using a RESPONSEpixx fiber-optic response box, hand-grip force via a MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs Inc., Philadelphia, USA; 100 Hz sampling), and pupil diameter via an MRI-compatible TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies, Montreal, Canada; 2000 Hz sampling). Stimuli were generated using Psychophysics Toolbox 3.0.18 [@brainard1997psychophysics; @kleiner2007s] in MATLAB R2022b (The MathWorks, Natick, MA). Data were collected inside an MRI scanner; neuroimaging results are reported elsewhere.

### Data Processing and Quality Control

**Reaction time definition.** In this response-signal design, reaction time (RT) was initially recorded as the latency from response-screen onset (“Same or Different?” prompt) to button press, termed **cue-locked RT**. However, perceptual evidence becomes available at probe onset (the second stimulus). To align RT with evidence accumulation onset, we derived **probe-onset-locked RT** by adding the fixed post-probe delay to cue-locked RT:

$$RT_{\text{probe-onset}} = RT_{\text{cue-locked}} + 0.35\text{ s}.$$ {#eq-probe}

where 0.35 s comprises 0.10 s probe duration plus 0.25 s grip-relaxation period. Probe-onset-locked RT served as the primary timing measure for DDM interpretation, as it aligns the decision process with evidence onset. Under this convention, the DDM non-decision time parameter ($t_0$) includes the fixed 0.35 s response-gating delay plus residual encoding and motor components. Cue-locked RT was retained for sensitivity analyses. This probe-onset-locked timing is our chosen convention to align $t_0$ with evidence onset; some DDM studies alternatively use cue-locked or response-locked reference points depending on task structure.

**Trial exclusion criteria.** To minimize the influence of premature or accidental button presses, trials with cue-locked RT < 0.20 s were excluded from the primary analysis. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using alternative cutoffs of 0.15 s and 0.25 s. Additional exclusions included missed responses, invalid run performance, and trials with non-positive or missing RT values. The same exclusion criteria were applied to both cue-locked and probe-onset-locked RT datasets (which differ only by the fixed 0.35 s offset). For pupil-linked DDM models, trials additionally required valid pupil data (see Pupillometry Preprocessing section). The data processing pipeline is summarized in @tbl-trial-exclusions.

To clarify the assumptions behind our RT definition, gating delay, and exclusion rules, we summarize the causal structure of the response-signal design and the hierarchical DDM in @fig-ddm-dag-plate. Panel A depicts a conceptual causal diagram in which Age and experimentally manipulated task factors (difficulty, modality, effort) influence latent DDM parameters, the wait constraint changes how latent decision completion maps onto observed RT, and RT-based exclusion is represented as conditioning on a selection node $S$. Panel B shows the corresponding generative structure of the hierarchical Wiener DDM, with subject-level parameters $v_i$, $a_i$, $T_{er,i}$ and trial-level predictors $X_{it}$ (difficulty, modality, effort) that generate choices and RTs. This figure separates our substantive causal assumptions from the statistical model used for estimation and highlights why RT cutoffs are treated as a potential source of selection bias in subsequent analyses.
